title: Persia and Its Empire
lead: The Achaemenid Persian Empire (about 550–330 BC), from Cyrus the Great to Darius III, ruled the Jews after Babylon fell. Its kings appear in Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Daniel, Haggai and Zechariah, and its habit of letting subject peoples keep their temples and laws under royal oversight shaped the world of the Second Temple.

sections.b:
Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC, and the Bible remembers him as the LORD's anointed who let the exiles go home (Isaiah 45:1; Ezra 1:1–4). Darius I let the temple be finished (Ezra 6), Xerxes is the Ahasuerus of Esther, and Artaxerxes I sent Nehemiah to rebuild Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah 2). Persian rule worked through satraps over large regions and governors over provinces; Judah (Yehud) was a small province inside the satrapy called Beyond the River, west of the Euphrates. Royal letters in Aramaic, the empire's official language, run through Ezra 4–7.

Outside the Bible the empire is known from the kings' own inscriptions (Behistun, Persepolis), the Cyrus Cylinder, thousands of clay tablets from Persepolis, business records from Babylonia, Herodotus, and the Aramaic letters of the Jewish soldiers at Elephantine in Egypt. These let historians test the Bible's picture of the Persian court, and on many details of titles, taxes and procedure they match it well.
